projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with William Shay was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran William Shay. Mr. Shay served in the U.S. Navy. He served on the Atlantic and the Pacific and in the Marians and Aleutian Islands. His highest rank was Seaman Second Class. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made in Mr. Shay's home in Madison, Ohio, on February 20, 2003. He was 78 at the time of this recording. MR. SWOPE: All right. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: I was living in Painesville, Ohio, going to Harvey High School at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were still in high school in December of 1941 --

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- when the attack on Pearl Harbor came?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What are your memories of that day?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, it was a really shocking, sad day for us all. And then shortly after that, for a number of reasons, I was restless and I decided to go and fight the Japs, so I left school without graduating. So in 1942, I signed up for six years in the Navy. And someone had told me, a friend of mine, he said that regular Navy has some preferences at times, and so I thought so I'll sign for six, whereas if I signed for -- just signed up in the Navy, they would keep me until time to let us out. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So how old were you when you signed up with the Navy?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Seventeen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was their cutoff?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, I had a working permit, so I -- and the recruiters were interested in recruiting, so we went through that through a working permit. It was a ways back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, the Navy training was to learn discipline and learn how to work with -- be a team. And so we'd learn about marching and seamanship and how to take care of our clothes, how to -- we had special ways of rolling our garments so -- we couldn't press them, so we rolled them, and then we'd unroll them and they looked like they had been pressed. We had sea bags and hammocks. When I went to Great Lakes for training, we had to sleep in those hammocks, which was not fun. They had metal stantions. Then you'd tie that, then every morning you had to secure that and lash it up in the proper manner. If you didn't and they called a end of ropes -- any piece of line they call it an Irish pendant. If your shirt tail was out, that was an Irish pendant. But, anyways, so you have to have it perfect or you'd get a gig. Then we had to clean the barracks. Then we had marching and then schooling. And we had athletic -- like marathons. We'd climb ropes and race and do all kinds of things. So that's basically what that was. So then I was to go to school and be a signalman, communications. So I had signed for that and I wanted that. And visual communications, flashing lights and flags and semifor, which is obsolete now, I found out in the last year or so. So that was about six weeks. So I went to the University of Illinois at Champagne-Urbana. That was the only college I went to. But they had a nice place to train there. They had a swimming pool and gymnasium area for fall weather. Then we worked outside with flag hoists. Big area, big gymnasium inside but a large track field outside with different masts like a ship would have with halyards and flags and we could send messages back and forth. We'd originate messages and learn the techniques of transmitting messages while underway or in port. So we did that. Then -- that was a nice place to be, by the way, the university, and we used the commissary there and what have you. So then I went to Philadelphia Navy yard, and I was to go on board the Battleship New Jersey. The New Jersey was in dry dock there and they were fitting the large guns at that time. In the meantime they needed destroyer escorts for the sailors, so they transferred me to another area in the Philadelphia yard there. Big yard, lots of Navy, lots of ships, and foreign ships, even. But, anyways, so then they had destroyer escort. These ships were used to -- all kinds of purposes. They would cost about half the price -- half of the price of a regular destroyer. They had modest armament compared to a destroyer but they could do everything, depth charges and 3-inch 50 guns.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How big were they compared to a destroyer?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, they were -- a destroyer, I can't tell you the length of it, but the average ship, DE was around 320 feet. We made them for Britain. We had a deal to make British destroyer escorts and they didn't have torpedo tubes. So the ship that I ended up on eventually was a DE-50 and it did not have tubes, torpedo tubes, launches, and so it was called a British DE. They were named after officers who lost their life in wartime.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the name of yours?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: USS Ankstrum. Ankstrum -- I forget. He was a lieutenant or something. And I forget the details of why they named it after him, but he was a hero. And so we went out on the destroyer escort, the men that would eventually end up on the DE-50, which was not finished. It was in the Navy yard being completed. And that ship drew about 8 foot of water, about 40-foot beam. Ours was 306 or 310 feet long, had 10, 20-millimeter machine guns, three 3-inch 50s, one quad 40, which was a pom-pom like antiaircraft. Then we had what they called a hedgehog, which threw -- looked like a bomb, aerial bomb. We could throw those over our bough and they would -- they would create a pattern in an attack on a submarine. And then we had two Y guns in the stern which were depth charge Y guns, and they would fire the depth charge to port and starboard, away from the ship. And then they had racks in the back, two racks that they could roll them just by pulling a lever and they'd roll them. And they set them for different detonation depths: shallow, deep, and very deep. And the man that was in charge of those had to set those according to the attack. So if we got a sound, picked up a sound, if we thought it was a submarine, the sound men would report that and we'd run on it. And then if we thought we had a good contact, when it was the best -- and that was like we -- a sound wave, and it would go beep-beep, and then the closer we got, it would go beep-beep-beep-beep real close, then they felt that we were over the target, we would then fire maybe the depth charges, all of them, that is, off the stern, off the -- each side of the ship and then maybe the hedgehog. Then the signalman, which I was up on the bridge, we had a canister like an oatmeal can and it was our job to throw that over the side so it -- in the nighttime it couldn't tell -- it was a marker. It would create a color, a big green color. So that's where we made our attack. So we could return to that and see that, if the water allowed us, it was smooth enough to see that. And so, anyways, back to the Navy yard. So we went on the ship and we each took our job on the ship that -- I was on the bridge as a signalman. A lot of times signalmen and quartermasters manned the helm. They traded off on the watch so they wouldn't get too weary and lose their course. Then we'd be on the bridge. If it was cold and the quartermaster had to go outside, you could warm up and be on the helm. But, anyways, we took the jobs with another sailor and he would tell us what function, the enunciator, the speed enunciator, the helm, the different terms used in -- helmsman would answer and respond to. And so we did that for a couple days, I forget, three days. Then we went aboard our ship, which was not finished. It was full of cables, electric cables and workmen, welders. But, nevertheless, they wanted to get us aboard, get accustomed to it. So then when it came time, they had a -- gosh, can't think of the name of it, but when the ship was commissioned --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A christening or --

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Commissioning, actually.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: No champagne or beer or anything. And so we're in the Navy yard there. Then they had dignitaries there finally the day. Then we raised the pendant to the top of the mast. The signalman's job was to handle all flags, and when you're in port or at anchor, you have what they call a jack at the bow the flag was flown at the stern. Underway the flag was athe masthead and the jack came down. And that meant -- and then if we were at anchor, we had to put up an anchor ball which was a large canvas bag, bigger -- twice the size of a basketball. That indicated that this ship was at anchor. And then when we came into port -- putting this all in perspective -- but when we came into port, we were usually challenged by the harbormaster. We'd send and signal and he'd challenge us. We had to learn all the signals, certain signals for different things. If you were an unknown ship, they would send AA-AA, which meant, Who are you? Then we would dash them back with a light and tell them who we were. And we'd also have usually our call name -- numbers up, DE-50 would be up so they could even see that. And then usually they'd give you weather and they'd give you your berth or where you were to dock. That was our job. And then as soon as we dropped anchor, the jack went up, the flag came down the mast and the stern flag went up, that sort of thing. What else can I say? So then after the Navy yard, the trials we went out on in the destroyer escort. We went to Bermuda on a shakedown. Prior to that, on our way we stopped in Yorktown, Virginia, and picked up depth charges and all our ammunition for our guns. And we had supplies aboard by then. We were in a division of four ships, four destroyer -- British-type destroyer escorts. It was called Com -- Com Court Division 14, I think. I can't remember. But we all had our call letters and our numbers. So then we went to Bermuda. And down there we fired at sleeves, target sleeves pulled by airplanes flown by. Then we had a submarine down there and we ran on the submarine and made -- so we used all our guns and everything, simulate runs on subs and targets of aircraft. And a lot of guys got drunk on rum and Coke, I remember, all the young men, not very old. There were old salts to oversee the new people. So there was always some older person in your division. So then we came back to Philadelphia and we were assigned a convoy we took through the canal, our division. One of our ships ran on a sub contact down there. We give them little credit for it. But that's all I can tell you about it. So we went through the canal. We stopped in Panama City. We went in two abreast, two of our vessels, and the convoy ships, who are wider, of course. And sometimes there were merchant men and Navy ships or transports, troop transport. And I don't remember what the particular convoy entailed but -- and I forget the number of ships. So then we went on to San Diego, dropped those ships off, then we went up by San Francisco. San Pedro, I think it was. And then we were outfitted to go to the Aleutians. We didn't know where we were going. Everybody said, "Where are we going?" So they put like sandpaper grips on the ladders and the decks so you wouldn't slip. It looked like emory cloth. Then they issued us foul weather gear. The word got out, scuttlebutt, that we're going to the Aleutians. So our division, so we took a convey there, and then we stayed up there for -- I think we were there a little over a year. And we worked in the Aleutian chain. Dutch Harbor, from Dutch Harbor to the end of the Aleutian chain. What did they call them? The Kuriles. But, anyways, we actually escorted a submarine once from Attu out towards Russia, out that way past all the islands, the last island. I don't know what their picket duty was to be out there but we were -- we were assigned to escort them. And they stayed on the surface until we left. Then we returned. So we would take supplies, men, and that was in 19 -- that would have been 1943. And that's -- that was after -- after the Battle of Attu. The Japs had invaded the island of Attu. They were in Kiska and they had a little sub base there, a little two-man submarine base. But that -- that skirmish was over when we got there. But we were bringing supplies and things back and forth, tankers and various things. And Adak was like the biggest island and most established. We had the best airport there. So we did put an airport on Attu, which -- and that was -- that was a bad battle for us. We lost a lot of soldiers. It was called Massacre Bay. And so that was a duty there. Roosevelt came up on the Baltimore, ship Baltimore. I don't have any war stories yet. We all had to get out in the weather and line the rail. Came up on the light cruiser, Baltimore. It was a big deal. Anyways, that was the duty we had. The ship's draft was only about -- less than 9 feet or less. So we had all the superstructure, masts, radar and everything. And so I think they were -- some nicknamed them the rollers. And in the Aleutians, in three days you had maybe one fair day. It was just -- you could -- you could count on it. So it was -- we didn't get dockage because they didn't have docks. So when we were at anchor, we were swinging back and forth. At anchor, swinging as well as pitching -- not pitching, rolling. So, anyways, that duty we had there. And then we had made some runs on what we thought were sub contacts. We were allowed to go ashore and see this sub base where the Japs had been. When we chased them out of there, they had ships in the harbor there where this sub base was and they sunk them, the various types of ships, and the masts were sticking out of the water. So we were there after the fact, which was all right with us. We didn't ask for that but we -- just so happened that our duty was -- we were fortunate to have that duty. So we got to know that -- that area pretty good back and forth. And we were refueling -- this is not a war story. We were refueling off a tanker, the Brazzo, it was a Navy tanker, and we were going to pass a message to them and we collided with them. We bumped. So that -- the enemy had left, so we didn't have to worry about that. Then we came back to the states, they sent us to the Marianas group.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you in the Aleutians?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Fifteen -- I think 15 months, yeah. So then we were sent into the Marianas, Guam, Saipan. Tinian is where all the B-29s, that's where they made the attack on Japan from. Tinian was an island you could see from Saipan. So we had the same type of duty there. And we had no problems. The Japs had been driven out of Saipan. They still had gun placements on the beach and they put pill boxes or -- on the banks there on the islands to ward off, you know, with American. So then we still hadn't shot down any enemy planes, so they sent us to -- gosh, my memory is slipping -- where we had the big -- the big battle. Jeez, you know, I can't think of the -- where they raised the flag.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Iwo Jima?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Iwo Jima. I'm trying to think of so many names. We were sent to Iwo Jima. We did picket duty around the island. At night -- this is another war story -- we're in there watching a movie and they're out there shooting parachutes, the marines, with flares, and you could see tracer bullets, and we're out in the safe harbor. So we had more good duty. We had picket duty there. And then we'd challenge airplanes as well as other ships that would come and we'd go around the island. They had a tower on Mount Sirbachi, I think they call it. That's where the tower was, the signal tower. Two times we had picked the pilots up that ditched their fighter planes. And so then we went -- we were back in Guam when the war was over. So that's my war stories.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever have any -- I don't suppose at that point any close encounters with kamikazes or anything like that?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: No, no. And we have this ships crew, we have reunions every year. We still do. We just had one this summer. And whoever says grace, sometimes I do, I always say that we were lucky that the duty we had put us in that we were out of harm's way. Somebody had -- I don't mean to say it that way. So we were fortunate. And those little DEs were used, kamikazes hit them. They were torpedoed. They were just -- you know, they were -- they were a tough little ship. But so we were fortunate. And I always say when we have a meeting that we're lucky we're here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No close calls with submarines or anything like that?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: No, no. So I don't have any good war stories to tell. And I don't make up stories so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you were in the Aleutians, were you quartered on board ship or did you have quarters on land?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: That ship was our home. That was our home. And they had what they called a supply ship. If we needed provisions, we would go. And if we -- the gun tubs, they were made -- I think three-eighths or less metal. The buffeting from the ocean would bend them in, so we'd go alongside and they'd repair those and we'd get to see a movie and get additional supplies. We had a -- they cost a half -- half the cost of a destroyer. And it was so simple. It was diesel electric. It was easy to manage and easy to use, economically, you know, the fuel. And we could get underway in five minutes if we had to. And so we had our mess, our quarters, fore and aft, and the officers had theirs. And so, yes, we lived on there. That was my home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there a problem with boredom among the guys?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: No, they -- they liked to gamble. I didn't gamble. And we had a guy played a mandolin. And we were kept pretty busy. Underway there was just watches, four on, then eight off. And out of that, you had duties. So it went pretty fast. You didn't have much spare time. Pretty good food. Food was okay. I was particular so I didn't eat as much but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How often did you get a new movie? You talk about movies.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: We had a movie maybe when we were in port down south. But in the Aleutians, once in awhile we'd have it, but if we went alongside a tender, it meant you might get some ice cream and you might get a Coke. And we had ability to transform sea water to fresh water. Evaporators, they called them, another name. So we had that ability, but we didn't -- we couldn't produce enough. They were -- always seemed to be -- they were cleaning them or something. So we could take a salt water shower, then rinse -- we had salt water soap. We could rinse in fresh water. So that was our hardship. When I'd see a rainstorm coming -- you could see it as it came across the water towards you down in the south. If I was off duty, I'd go get my towels and I'd get under the scupper and aft and the gun tub. So we were lucky sailors, all of us. And we still have these reunions, we get together. And we had a national get-together for destroyer escort sailors in South Carolina this summer. There was about a thousand of us, some from England and Scotland. So we realize how fortunate we were. So I don't have any good --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that a reunion of all destroyer escort crews, basically?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, yes, throughout the country.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Not just your division or anything?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: No, no. And we go there and muster. And they have speakers and dinner and they even had a dance, things like that. Some guys had made models of ships that were powered by radio control, about 8-foot long. They put them in the water. They had all kinds of -- then you could play golf. So it's --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies on board the ship?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: A few, very few. One of my closest friends passed away. I still have a few that I send Christmas cards to so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you do anything in particular with them for entertainment?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, there we did. We saw a couple of nice shows. I can't remember the name of them, but we went to those. And we mustered together. And they were in the same hotel, on the same floor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where was that?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Not Hilton Head.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh --

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: South Carolina.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: South Carlonia, right.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Just the beach area there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Hilton Head, I guess, right?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: No. No. The famous area there. So they decided to go there, whoever picked that out. And there were dice activities. Then the captain lives there, so we went to his home on the beach, and so it's nice. Then we trade stories and how everybody's doing. And I paint a little bit and these are my paintings. So I painted a ship. I was going to show it to you -- I had it in the other room -- of our ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When Roosevelt came did he deliver a speech to the guys?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: No. We were on board ship. So whoever -- I imagine he stayed on the ship and the commanders in that area, senior officers afloat, I don't know who they would be, whether they're admirals or vice admirals, probably went aboard the Baltimore. And what his purpose was, I'm not sure. Didn't build my morale, really, necessarily. So then when they left the Baltimore, light cruiser, we had top speed of 22, 23 if we were lucky, and they had us go out, escort them out of the harbor. And they always felt that was a vulnerable time. Where ______ was in -- I think that was Amchitka where Bob was, they had nets, and they would draw them across the harbor entrance at night, and Adak, I forget, some of the others. So if you got there too late at night, they wouldn't let you in and you had to stay out at sea. And so we'd try to govern our arrival at the right time. Then in the morning they open them at dawn. So, anyways, we took -- went out with the Baltimore and I wished I'd have kept the message. They said some kind of joke. The captain of the ship said, "If you can't keep up," you know, something. But they made a little joke out of it. Our old ship's just steaming along and the pinnacles vibrating. But, anyways, so that's all I know about the President. But that was an interesting --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember the day FDR died?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Vaguely.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There wasn't a big reaction on board ship?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: No, no. No, that -- we got news -- they used to send out a little Time magazine. Time, and what's the other?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Look, maybe?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: No, Time and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Or Life?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Life, no. Anyways, nice little -- with important events that happened. So we didn't get too much news. We just -- nowadays I think my grandson's on a ship and they're dropping mail off on his way over to Kuwait, and they have email. They're sending email back and forth. So it's a different --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember mail call on board your ship?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes, indeed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And what kinds of things would they send from home to you?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, I had a girlfriend and she sent a lot of mail and sometimes the mail didn't catch up with us. So, man, they'd call my name six, seven times. Some guys, I don't think they called their name at all. They'd say, "Mail call" and we'd all go out on the -- if it was foul weather, we'd be below deck and if it was good weather, we'd be outside. And then some guys would pass the mail back. So I didn't get too many packages but I got a lot of mail. {Interview interrupted by a telephone call.}

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: We went ashore, see, we came back with souvenirs. So that's a grotesque --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So this is a Japanese skull?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yes, from Attu. A couple guys got sabers and then they had ammunition boxes and things, souvenirs. So I brought this back and I painted on it. I was -- I was privileged to see all the charts on the bridge. And so I drew a map of Attu Bay and Massacre Bay and I lettered it and I put a big red cross there and I put the dates on there. I wanted to send it home and they wouldn't let me. So, anyways, we got back to the states, I had it painted. This is porous, this skull, you know. A guy sprayed it in the Navy yard there. But that's a grotesque souvenir, huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you put it in your duffle bag to bring it back?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: You bet. That's a gruesome thing, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's the first I've seen.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: So I've shown it to my grandchildren. Then I -- I painted, actually painted it. I did it in a paint class that I had. I painted that. These are my paintings here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there a lot of other souvenir collecting throughout the whole time you were there?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: That was about the only place we were at where we could get souvenirs like that. In Saipan I had a picture taken of me and the -- one of those pill boxes on the side of the hill and I had a femur bone in my hand. So I'm kind of a ghoul, huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Interesting anatomy.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: And then on the guns, there was about a 4-inch gun, I think they had Japanese stampings, you know, that -- gun makers, and so I made -- I put paper on it and I, you know, made tracings of it just as a souvenir. But I can't think of anything else that I was near. When we went ashore, I was curious. I wanted to see where they had the submarine base. It was a nice little cove there. They used crates to build -- they used crating, you know, like we would throw away a burnt up -- they used crating to build structures, a tunnel back in there. And they had some lead weights that were about like this, and I bet they weighed 20 pounds, that thick, ingot-like. So we didn't have -- we have sound -- sound equipment to tell us how deep the water is and we didn't have that on -- we didn't have any sounding. So sounding weights were used, you know, in the rivers in olden days, so I took this back as a sounding wave. We worked with a geodatic ship. We would -- we'd work off of one another. We were mapping that area. We did a lot of that duty. We must have done -- I'll bet we did a week of that. And so one time we anchored in the ocean. I can't remember how close we were to land, but we drifted. In the morning we found out we had been drifting. We had two anchors out and the anchors got crossed, twisted. So we could have drifted into the beach, onto the rocks. So I got this lead line out, I told the officer, I said to the -- Kroger was his name, "Lieutenant," I said, "I got a way we can sound and then we'll know if we're drifting or not." So they really didn't have anything to take -- to scan with the radar, you know. They could have but I guess we just thought we were secure. But that -- something bad could have happened with that. That's the reason I brought the lead back. I was going to -- and lead lines are made up in 6-foot -- a fathom is 6 foot. So then you have different markings on there, leather, red, you know, white rags and things that tell you how many fathoms when you hit the bottom. We never did use it but -- so that's a souvenir. I dragged that heavy thing back. So I was -- did lettering. I've done some sign work. The college -- sign at Lake Erie College, carved sign, Jim Polacheck (ph) is an ex-fireman. Bob and I went in the fire service in 1950. That's how Bob and -- and we were in school together, for that matter. Now, I beat him at golf. He'll tell you the opposite. So I went to work for this sign carver. I was interested in that. And so everything that needed lettering on the ship, I got the job, you know. So like they had a locker with publications that were restricted and I had to print on there. So that was one of my hobbies on the ship. But I just don't have any great stories to tell.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you on VJ day?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: In Guam.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any particular celebrations on that day?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, a lot of whistle blowing, the kind where you pull at lanyard. A lot of that. And nobody cared. The officers would -- you'd get -- take two liberties away from you if you pulled that lanyard any other time. So, yeah, that was a good place to be. And we were -- we were at anchor there. And then guys on the ship, they wanted -- below decks, they could come up on the bridge. And other ships there. But that was it. I was regular Navy. I got married in 19- -- when I came home from Guam I forget how long it was before we came back to the states. Of course, we always stopped in Hawaii. And then I got married but I still had time to serve in the Navy. I had lots of points but I couldn't get out, so that was a mistake. So I was married in 1945 and my son was born a year later and I'm over in China. So I got married. I had about a -- I had over a month off; not because I earned that but because they were trying to find a place to send me. So I was home here in Cleveland. I stayed in a hotel and the government paid for it. We stayed down there for, oh, gosh, nine days, my wife and I. We were on our honeymoon, of course. So then each day I had to check in. So finally they sent me back out west on a train. She went along and they paid for it. Then we stayed together in California a little while. Then they sent me on a troop ship to Shanghi. It was Sea Runner, troop transport converted from a transport ship. So I spent time in China, Shanghi, and then I went to Singtow. And when my son was born, I asked to get out of the Navy. So I actually served almost six -- almost -- five years, a little less than five years, and I asked to get out. A friend of mine, he said, "I'm going home." And I said, "How are you going to do that?" And he said, "Well, I'm getting a dependency discharge." So I got to thinking, my son is born and I haven't seen him -- the mail didn't catch up with me when we left Shanghi. I was on a tug then and I was on flag ships, and then I went to this tug because there was 17 guys and no regimen, no dress uniform, no dress up, no -- so I traded with a guy and got that job. Well, they sent us to Singtow, nice place. The Germans had been in Singtow and it was just a beautiful place. Looked like Bermuda. A lot of brick roofs and they had a big observatory on the top hill there. But, anyways, then I made this application. I had to have something from my minister, something from somebody that knew me and saying I'd be better off home with my son and my wife. So I got that. Then the pictures came for my son that he had -- caught up in my mail. So I came home on a ship. It was a -- it was the Le June. It was a pretty fast little cruise ship converted and painted, you know, all painted and pools covered. So my duty was just to wash my underwear at night and take a shower. Then I came home and I took my discharge at -- near Verbuna (ph), California, and got a flight home. It was hard to get flights then but someone, minister or something that somebody knew that was in Oakland got me a flight home. So I came home and then I ended up in the fire department, anyways, with Bob.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Overall did you like your time in the Navy?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yes, I like the Navy. Like the regimen. I like the sea. I like the water. When we were in harbor, I'd go off and explore. I was allowed to. We were at a dock in -- where were we then? Not Anchorage but Dutch Harbor, Alaska. There was a ship in there that had been broke in half and they towed to -- I forget which half they towed in there but it was over there. Merchant ship. So went over there in a little skip I borrowed and I cut a big piece of canvas. You know what a coracle is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A coracle?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yeah. That's what the people over in -- I guess in the Sahara area there, people are on the water, they have these little skin-covered round -- like a tam, a man's hat or a woman's hat. So I was going to make one of those so when we came into port I could get in there and paddle around. I went over on that ship, cut a big piece of canvas off the top of the deck with my knife, rolled it up, and then I was going to make this coracle so that the framework, I'd put it in there and then drawstring that and tie it. Then I could put it under the gun tub in the back of the ship. So I was always exploring and picking up traps and seeing how many lobsters were in there, calm, nice days.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When was that where you were catching the lobsters?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Dutch Harbor, Alaska. The traps were there, you know. You could see them. You could pull them up and, you know, right in the inner harbor there, you see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you got to eat a lot of lobster up there?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, no, no. I didn't steal them, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: These were the fishermen's traps?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But did they buy lobster or anything? Did you ever --

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: No. No, we never had --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Stuck with the Navy food?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: We were underway on Thanksgiving so we couldn't eat because it was too rough, you know. So we postponed that. It was about four days later we had it. We always had big meals on Christmas and Thanksgiving. That was a treat. So we just postponed it is all. So that was the hardship I had.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about that whole experience, does any other particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: No. I was young and fearless. We didn't think about being in the cold water or anything. Liked the duty, liked -- and the messages, they came in and if we were in port, coming out of off duty with a convoy, say, from Attu to Adak, that's three days, we -- they'd give us time off. We'd refuel and a water barge could come alongside and a fuel barge. We refueled at sea one time. That's quite a feat, down in the south. And so I liked the sea. And as the signalman, after we were in there, we'd get the message, pretty soon it'd come. We'd get the weather two or three times a day. And then when we were to take another convoy, the message would come to the signalman on duty. So it would say -- the heading would be the date and who originated it, the time and everything, and then it would say who it's information to. So if we had a convoy of two DEs and four -- a tanker and some other things or whatever, they'd be named in there. And then they'd usually have a meeting. The officers would gather on one of the ships and they'd have a meeting about how they're going to do it and what our courses would be. We'd zig-zag. So we knew where we were going before the officer of the deck did. So we were important. Come down, I'd have this pad -- or any one of the signalmen, the OD'd come down on the deck, be on the deck, lower deck, and guys say, "Where we going? Where we going?" They knew we had a message. "What's up? What's new?" So that's one thing we did learn first. So we were on the know, in other words, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your highest rank?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: I was a signalman third class. I had got in trouble in Frisco, got drunk and argued with an officer and went to the brig for five days and lost a stripe. So, anyways --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That happen a lot with the crew? Did they get into trouble?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Not too often. Not too often. You get some fights sometimes. I guess they get restless. Then sometimes they'd get some alcohol. When we were in Dutch Harbor, Chief Boltson, an oldtimer, went ashore. The Marines were in charge of who went in and out of Dutch Harbor. That's very primitive then. Go into a bar and floor is dirt, hard-packed dirt, some hookers in there. So to go into this town, there was an embankment that came down and then there was a shanty there. It was actually a Quonset hut in the middle of the road and then you go in one side and out the other, then down like this and then there's more water on that side. So the guys bought liquor, of course. The Marines would rap them, you know, in their stomachs or in their socks and break the bottles. Or they'd take them and throw them on the bank. And you could see all the labels there were. They wouldn't let the guys have it. And I guess they got a kick out of that. That was your job. So they inspected you. They had big semi trailers, they called them cattle cars, and they had big doors. You just stepped on it like a bus, just stepped on there. They would take you to and from your ship. So this Boltson had a fifth of liquor in his belt, evidently -- I wasn't there when it happened, but they always had officer of the deck and a petty officer of the deck. So when the Boltson came on, the tide had changed. I think -- I remember that the most it ever changed was about 3 foot there when we were there getting on and off. And if it was more -- the tide was big up there, but this one was a 3-foot. So he jumped down. There was enough -- that was the point I wanted to make. He jumped down, the bottle fell. And the OD was -- I remember his name, Lieutenant Porter. He was a prick. He -- he went in to get a witness and it was the Boltson and a junior petty officer there, he went and got a broom to clean up. He did it for two reasons, primarily to clean up the mess. So then the evidence went through the scupper, you know. The scupper is about that wide. So he just pushed it in the water between the dock and the ship. So he got a pilot to defend him. So he beat that rap. I don't know if he had to pay the -- the Air Force lieutenant was an attorney. But we did a lot of drinking up there, you know, onshore. And we hadn't been drinking, we hadn't been -- we could get beer but not whiskey, so a lot of guys got really -- got --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get along okay with the officers overall, though?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Oh, yes, yes. They were okay. Kroger was a guy looked like Errol Flynn. He was affiliated with the Kroger store.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Flying fish would fly -- get in the gun tubs. He'd send the mess men up there to gather them up and they'd prepare them for dinner. He was -- he was -- did some -- and then one time there was a whale floundering in the Aleutians. So I'm on the bridge as signalman and I hear him and he says, "Get the gunner's mate to bring me a rifle," chief gunner. So he brings him a rifle and he shoots this whale. He's shooting and the whale moves a little bit. Kind of an unorthodox guy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was he hungry or did he just shoot the whale?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Just an unusual guy. Good lookin' son of a -- and if you're on watch with him at night, it would be you and the lock-outs and another signalman. He'd talk just nice as could be. But the next day you walk down the deck, he didn't know you. But, yeah, they were that way. They were nice. They were in the same situation we were. So as I said, I feel very lucky and our crew that we -- we had that kind of duty. And a lot of the DEs were -- they were really mutilated and their crews. They used -- after the war, I can't remember -- you know, I've got some interesting literature. Maybe you'd -- I don't know if it's -- it's about the nomenclature of the ships and what they were used for. I don't know if you'd like to refer to that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: If you have copies of that, that would be great.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, I don't know if I could forego the material but it's -- really tells you a lot of things that I mentioned. Tells about the -- what their purpose was, antisubmarine. They even had crews in World War II that went out with a carrier and there would be destroyer escorts. They'd go searching for submarines. They work as a group. So we moved all troop ships, tankers. They had many duties. They could utilize them in many ways. I have some literature, maybe you'd like to look at it. I don't know if somehow you could get it back to me, I'd like to retain it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I've got some things you're going to have to send me anyway. What are we talking about, a book or --

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Just some printed sheets.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Little printed pages?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: If it would fit in, you could send it to me.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: I'm sure you could derive something out of there. And you'll have to realize that it was a long time ago, all this. But, as I said, I said to Bob, I said, "What can I tell that guy?" And he said, "Well, make up some good lies."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you didn't, right?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I don't think any of the guys I talked to have lied. There's been some question about that, that they're afraid that veterans will make up stories. I've talked to 120 guys and I'm 99.9 percent sure I've heard the truth.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: A lot of guys in the bars talk about things they did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But when they sit down and record it, they tell the truth.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I mean, yes, I think there are a lot of people that fabricate or exaggerate stories. You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: I think -- yeah, I don't -- like I say, I wish I had something --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, it's very interesting. I'm never going to forget the skull.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yeah, don't forget that. You should have seen it. It was really nice. So Kroger says, "You can't send that home." So I had this little map on top and I -- you know what a Maltese cross looks like?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Sure.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, it was a red Maltese cross there and Massacre Bay and the drawing in India ink of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, you had to paint that over because it was too much information or --

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, no. I guess later it didn't mean so much, so one day I painted some more over it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's kind of a shame. It would have been interesting.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yeah, I should have left that on there. I don't think I have any real good story. We never had any problems. We never had any serious, you know, dangerous positions. That time we drifted and the anchors got tangled, the captain was right down there working with them -- surprised us all -- with his sleeves rolled -- not really because it was cold but -- so, very fortunate. Well, trying to think of -- then I got around, you know. And on the tug, I liked that tug duty. And we had a Chinaman on there, little China guy. I suppose he was 22, and he'd cook for us. And we ate on plates. I could order two eggs, three eggs, four eggs. And that was in Shanghi. We were at dock. Then we went to Singtow. We took -- two tugs went and an LCI, infantry landing craft. I was going to say, they moth-balled a lot of these ships. We were going to build a thousand or something. Roosevelt then got down to it was only 500 that we built. And they were modeled after frigots that the British had. But, anyways, then we gave some to the Chinese, some of our ships. That was easier than bringing them home. So the Chinese Navy used them. And destroyer -- I can't remember who else we gave some to, Turkey or something, other countries like that, made some kind of deal. But they moth-balled a lot of them. I have pictures of them, mothball version, in a magazine or something. But the Navy, like you asked me, I was young. I just got my diploma last winter.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your high school diploma?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yeah. I always was self-conscious about that. But restless. My parents had divorced. I had two other brothers. And it just seemed -- you know, then they said join the Navy and learn a trade. Well, when I got out, what can you do with two semifor flags? So -- but I enjoyed the Navy and it was good discipline. I think all young men should be in the service for a year. I guess Switzerland has some kind of deal where their men all have to serve. So that part was good. And then all I did after that was make babies. And I went -- as I say, went in the fire service when Bob did. And then when I retired, I had a little painting business and then I went into that sign painting. And I started to say, that sign at the college, that carved sign, I wanted to learn to carve, so Jim Polacheck took me on. I said, "If you ever need some help." So then I learned to carve. That was one of our first signs, the college, the big sign. And it was an emblem on there, the college, what would they call the insignia of the college. It's a rope roping around the Bible. I don't know if that's a Bible. I don't know what it is. But it's an open book. And that was hard to do. We had to do both sides. The wood was mahogany, 2 inches thick. So we had to plane that wood, glue it up, shape it, then cut the shape. So I really loved that. And I like to do -- I learned to lay goldleaf. So I worked with him until my back gave out. I had a back operation a year and a half ago, so I couldn't do that. Once you finished a sign, you had to put it in the ground, had to dig some holes, auger the hole. So it was too much for me. Bob and I are 78 years old now. And so I had that -- I was in a wheelchair, went on a cruise through the canal. I wanted to go through the canal again. And my sweetheart, she wanted to go, too. So we get down there to get on this ship and my legs are rubbery. I had signed up for an operation in May and we went in April, and two-week cruise through the canal. Got down there and my legs gave out on me. I had some of that before and I had seen this doctor and I had had a lot of therapy but it didn't seem to work. So I had stenosis of the spine. Well, anyways, we signed up for May 4th. So got down there and I said, "Lillian," I said, I said, "jeez," I said, "my legs are giving out on me. I'm going to go over and lean against that pole there. When this big long line gets up there, I'll join you." She says, "Sit on the floor." I had shorts on. I said, "I'm not sitting on that dirty floor." I had white shorts on. So by the time she got up there, then I managed to get to the counter where we checked in, then I asked for a wheelchair. So finally a wheelchair came and put me on and the elevator brought me up. The ramp that goes onto the ship -- have you ever been on a cruise?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: You better go.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: It's the best way to spend your money. Then the gangway is quite an angle. So this older gent, you know, pushing me -- I weighed 190 pounds then -- and pushed me up there and got in the room and I thought, Well, tomorrow I'll be fine. Two weeks I was in that damn wheelchair. One, not that same one. And the ship was new and the carpet was -- it was called -- fancy name but brand new. The carpet was thick. Then every threshold -- every compartment had a threshold about that wide and it was high and it was made of stainless. So she had to pull me over that. So that was a sad scene. But we saw a lot of the canal. When I was in the Navy, I think I slept through some of that when we went through there in the Navy. But I had the operation in May. June, July -- August I started hitting the golf ball in the back yard. There was no houses back here so I could -- hit two or three, the next day I thought, Jesus, that was okay. So then --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long did it take to go through the canal back then when you went through during the second world war?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: I can't tell you. We did it -- I don't know how long it was that we did it. It was daytime, so a lot to see. When we got to Balboa, we stopped there for fresh provisions. I had a nice coin here. They had the nicest money. It has a picture of Balboa on it. I just had the coin here the other day. It was the prettiest money. I have these curtains up. You know why? Because I couldn't keep my house warm. Jeez, I wish I could show you that coin. I just moved it. It has a picture of Balboa with that helmet on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: So I think I'm going to drill a little hole in that. I got different denominations. So we stayed there all day and night, then took off the next morning, so I can't tell you how long it took. But -- and when we were on the cruise ship, we just had a -- I don't think we had much more room than that on the side. I'm not exagerating. Seemed like maybe 18 inches. They're designing ships, you know, to get through the canal. They make them narrower. Too big, you can't get through there. So it saves a lot of money. And -- so I had a lot of experiences in the Navy and, as I said, I liked it and -- but I just wanted -- the war was over and I wanted to get home, and so I did. But I didn't learn anything in there. So then when I got home, I did different things. While in the Navy, I was interested in my diploma, so I signed up for -- I can't remember the name of it but it's a famous course that -- correspondence course, one of the first and biggest. So I sent away to do my schooling through international correspondence school. There's a name that goes with it. Not Anderson but something. But it was hard to concentrate on the ship. I'd be down there and the guys would say, "What are you doing," you know. You'd send in your work and then they'd send you back a grade and more work and a plate. They called them plates, I think. But I never developed a -- so it's bothered me that I didn't finish high school. And then recently -- I'll go get my diploma and show it to you. So it's always bugged the hell out of me but I don't know how much it would have meant. So I took the GED test after awhile -- how long I was home, I guess 1975 I got divorced -- and I rated 11th grade. So that made me feel pretty good. So I had to touch up on math, I think, and I forget -- then you get to go back, you can go back as many times as you want. But I was too lazy. I'd rather go to Florida. And so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you finally did it.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yes. Put the hat on me and the whole works so -- and I go to all the class reunions and they don't remember, you know. But it did bother me because I didn't have that. And like I said, I knew that but how many people, they don't remember me back then. So we still have reunions, and that goes back a ways, you know, 1943. So I drew maps of places. Pencil, that's all I had. This, Errol Flynn was up there, Adak Island, Deduct (ph) Straits, and then I had maps of --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So Errol Flynn was there, huh?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Yeah, he came up there to entertain the troops. And the different monies --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any other USO shows that you remember?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: In the University of Illinois, Coca-Cola paid bands and they came in the auditorium. Big bands, you know, and ones at Great Lakes. I forget what it was. My grandson's a captain in the Marine Air Force. He's on this -- in this group that will arrive in the next two or three days -- two days, I think. He'll be in Kuwait. And he was in Afghanistan. He was on the Pellalou. That's the ship that had that traitor, that young fella, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, what's his name?

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Walker.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: John.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Walker, yeah. But he was on the Pellalou. And that ship, the Pellalou, is like an aircraft carrier. The stern is open and they launch boats. They have hovercrafts and boats launch. It's an attack ship. And then they had -- he flies a CH-46, a big, two-prop helicopter. Then they have the windows up in the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: I can't remember the name of those smaller helicopters, but the complete ship. So he had a taste of that. Now he's over -- going to end up in Kuwait.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let's hope nothing happens.

sp.speaker: William Shay
sp.p: Well, nice of you to come out.
